title: continuous-profiling-agent-integration
content:
Purpose and status:

This doc captures a pragmatic approach to integrating a continuous profiling agent into the serving runtime CI and nightly pipelines. The goal is to get low-noise, actionable profiles that can be compared across commits and pinned to commits/releases, with automated flamegraph generation and lightweight alerts for regressions. This is a working doc, audience: eng-serving-runtime and eng-observability.

Design principles:
- Keep production overhead under 1% p99 for CPU during normal traffic by sampling and adaptive duration.
- Prefer safe, out-of-process collectors where possible (eBPF userland collector or async-profiler attached via sidecar) to avoid heap corruption and runtime interference.
- Store compressed profile artifacts with commit metadata and a deterministic path for automated comparison.
- CI should produce diff reports for perf regressions on PRs and nightly baselines for long-term trend detection.

Components and responsibilities:
- Collector agent: lightweight eBPF sampler for system-level, and async-profiler for Java/Py runtimes. Eng-serving-runtime owns the config.
- Upload service: simple lambda that ingests profiles to s3 with metadata. Eng-platform owns retention rules.
- Compare job: perf-compare tool that consumes two profile blobs and emits a change summary and flamegraph delta. Eng-observability owns the comparator.
- Alerting: metric-based alerts if a regression is detected by comparator above threshold. Eng-sre to own alert ops.

Naming and storage conventions:
- s3 path: s3://redwood-profiles/serving-runtime/{branch_or_release}/{commit_sha}/{node-id}/{timestamp}.prof.gz
- Metadata file next to profile: metadata.json containing commit, branch, k8s pod, git ref, build id, kernel, runtime version, sampling config

CI integration (PR-level):
- On Linux runners that can run perf tools, run a 'micro-benchmark harness' for the change candidate for N seconds and collect cpu profiles. Use docker image perf-runner:latest.
- Steps (high level):
  1) spin up a small cluster using kind or use prebuilt runner with a local service binary
  2) run workload replay for 30s to 120s depending on signal-to-noise
  3) run collector in sampling mode, output to /tmp/profile.prof
  4) upload profile artifact to s3 staging path with PR id
  5) run comparator against baseline commit profile and attach a short html report to PR

Example CI snippet (bash):

# start collector sidecar (eBPF-collector)
/opt/profiler/bin/ebpf-collector --target-pid $(pidof serving-runtime) --duration 60 --sample-rate 199 > /tmp/profile.pb && gzip -c /tmp/profile.pb > /tmp/profile.prof.gz

# upload
aws s3 cp /tmp/profile.prof.gz s3://redwood-profiles/serving-runtime/pr-1234/$(git rev-parse HEAD)/node-01/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).prof.gz --acl private

# compare to baseline
perf-compare --left s3://redwood-profiles/serving-runtime/baseline/abc123/profile.prof.gz --right /tmp/profile.prof.gz --out /tmp/pr-1234-perf-report.html

Nightly aggregation job (k8s cronjob):
- Run collector across a small set of canary pods for 5 minutes at reduced sample rate during a quiet window.
- Aggregate samples across three pods and emit an aggregated folded stack file.
- Generate flamegraph svg and upload to s3 under nightly/ branch/commit.

Flamegraph generation (local):
- Use stackcollapse and flamegraph.pl from Brendan Gregg utilities (or perf-tools compatible). Example:
  1) convert raw perf to folded stacks: perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > folded.stacks
  2) generate svg: flamegraph.pl folded.stacks > flame.svg

Lightweight comparator heuristics:
- Focus on top N stacks contributing to p50/p90/p99 CPU time.
- Use normalized delta: (new - old)/old for each stack and surface only stacks exceeding 20% relative increase and absolute > 50ms total time.
- Produce summary: total CPU time increase, top 5 regressors, likely file/line hints.

Operational runbook notes (quick triage):
- If collector fails on a pod: check kernel headers and eBPF subsystems, run ebpf-collector --check
- If profiles look empty: check sampling rate, container isolation, ptrace disablement. For containerd, ensure securityContext allows ptrace where needed or use eBPF which avoids ptrace.
- High overhead observed: reduce sample rate and increase run duration, switch to stack sampling mode rather than jstack style.

Troubleshooting snippets:
- Check process view: ps -eo pid,cmd,etime | grep serving-runtime
- Check ebpf agent logs: kubectl logs profiler-collector-foo -n infra
- Reproduce locally: run minimal binary with LD_PRELOAD profiling shim or run under docker with SYS_PTRACE capability

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decide long-term on a single collector tech for all runtimes vs hybrid. eBPF is promising but needs kernel compatibility matrix documented.
- Thresholds for CI-level vs nightly-level comparisons need tuning. Start with 20%/50ms and iterate.
- Add traces correlation: tie CPU hotspots to trace spans in console for quicker root cause. Requires instrumentation mapping between function addresses and service spans.

References and links:
- perf-compare prototype repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/perf-compare
- async-profiler docs: https://github.com/jvm-profiling-tools/async-profiler
- Brendan Gregg flamegraph tools: https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph

Notes to self:
- try a 2 minute sample at 199Hz on canary and compare signal quality vs 30s at 997Hz
- capture kernel version and libc symbolization step for every upload

Contact: Maya Chen for questions on config and PR workflow.
